spec.description: All the captures at their finest, as Esri stores them. A browser reads only the tiles in view.
spec.title: Splats on Esri

options.content:
**What it shows.** Building E, an office building on Esri's campus in Redlands, California, as it went up: eight drone flights over its site, from May 2019, the ground cleared, to March 2022, the building in use, each turned into a Gaussian splat scan. Two of them stand side by side from the same viewpoint: pick a month in Capture for the left map and in Compare with for the right one, or click a month in the table (Compare puts it on the right). Each map has its own camera: drag with the right button (or Ctrl and drag) to tilt and turn it; the maps let you come as close as about 10 m.

**What a Gaussian splat is.** A photographic 3D scene made of millions of small coloured ellipsoids, each with its own size, turn and opacity, fitted to a drone's photographs so that, drawn together from any side, they look like the photographs. Thin things (a steel frame, a fence, a lift's boom) come out as they are seen, where a mesh would have to model them as surfaces.

**Where they come from.** Esri publishes every capture on ArcGIS Online as OGC 3D Tiles 1.1: glTF tiles with the Khronos extension `KHR_gaussian_splatting`, their splats compressed with SPZ, at several levels of detail, 80 to 170 MB each at their finest; your browser reads from Esri only the tiles in view. Two were made by Esri's drone team with Drone2Map 2025.2 and published with "Public demo + Distribution Rights" ("This dataset can be demoed and shared publicly"): [19 September 2019](https://www.arcgis.com/home/item.html?id=5cd49045be9a4a28a46ea74ce268a4d2), 178 photographs from a DJI drone with a Zenmuse X4S, and [21 February 2021](https://www.arcgis.com/home/item.html?id=e611bf9097f24c40a6925d5e388a523a), 664 photographs from a Freefly Astro with a Sony A7R II. The six others come from Esri's public web scene [Building E Gaussian Splats](https://www.arcgis.com/home/item.html?id=ca04bb941f9941739bf8075fe8d503ac), made with Site Scan for ArcGIS; their items name the month only and no licence (that scene has a September 2019 capture too: the one shown here is the drone team's). What each capture shows, in the table, is our reading of the scans.

**How it is drawn.** By Kepler Plus's Gaussian Splats layer, in the browser with WebGL: each splat as the ellipse it covers on the screen, fading from its centre, sorted from far to near and blended. Each scan is set on the map's ground by its own lowest splats: the site stands some 350 m above sea level, and until its first tiles arrive a scan is held by the middle of its bounds, so it can come into view at all.

**What to expect.** A drone looks down: roofs, slabs and the yard are sharp, walls under eaves less so, the steel frame a little soft where its members are thinner than the photographs could resolve. The first view of a month takes a few seconds while its coarse tiles arrive; the finer ones follow as you come closer. The satellite picture under the scans is today's.
